Two years after his mother died, after four winters of her illness, Ivan began volunteering at the hospice on the edge of Bergen every Thursday evening. He read newspapers aloud to Mr Olsen, helped families find the coffee machine, and sat with people who didn't want to be alone at night. He was good at it. The nurses said he had a calm that couldn't be taught.

Ingrid, the volunteer coordinator, noticed something else. Ivan never took the chair by the window, the one like the chair in his mother's ward. And after Mr Olsen died, Ivan came in the next Thursday as if nothing had happened.

"You're allowed to miss your own mother here too," Ingrid said quietly, handing him coffee. Ivan held the cup a long time. "I thought this was how I was doing that."
"It's part of it," she said. "Not all of it."

qa.a: Ivan read newspapers aloud to Mr Olsen.

qa.q: Why might hospice work feel meaningful to Ivan?
qa.a: Ivan's grief for his mother found a purpose in comforting others, which made the loss feel less helpless, even while the sadness itself stayed unspoken.

qa.q: How might Ingrid see Ivan's calm?

grounding: Shows a man who lost his mother to a long illness finding purpose in hospice work, while his own grief still needs room.

In the skills lab of the nursing college in Nagpur, Chaitanya was first to volunteer for every practical: blood pressure, bed baths, the careful way to turn a patient without hurting them. He had learned most of it already, in two years of nights beside his father's hospital bed.

"That's why I joined," he told his classmate Nirmala. "So someone else's Baba gets what mine got at the end. Good care."

Nirmala watched him on their first ward posting. He was steady with every patient until they reached the long-stay unit. There he stopped at the door, hand on the frame, and went very pale.

Later, in the canteen, she said, "You can be a great nurse and still need to grieve him, you know. The college counsellor has hours on Fridays."

Chaitanya stirred his tea. "Maybe Friday," he said.

Dear Mehak,

You asked why I signed up for the palliative care course after Ammi. I've been trying to answer that for a month.

For three years we learned things nobody should have to learn: how to turn her gently, how to wet her lips when she couldn't drink, how to sit quietly when she was scared at night. When she died I kept thinking all of it would just vanish. Now I use it every Saturday at the care centre in Hyderabad, with other people's mothers. It feels as if she's still teaching me.

But honestly, last week an old lady there hummed the song Ammi used to hum, and I had to leave the room. I sat in the car for half an hour. The work helps. It doesn't do my missing her for me.

Can we visit her grave together when you're home in June?

Your brother,
Yusuf

When Rafiq's turn came to read aloud in Class 4, he stumbled on "mysterious". "Mys... mister... mystery-ous?" Somebody at the back snorted.

Before the snort could grow, Rafiq crossed his eyes, puffed out his cheeks and said in a robot voice, "MY-STER-I-OUS. Word defeated me. Rafiq shutting down." The whole class burst out laughing, and he grinned and bowed.

His friend Imran laughed hardest. But at lunch Imran noticed Rafiq quietly practising the next page under the desk, lips moving, finger on each word.

"You're doing the robot tomorrow too?" Imran asked.

"Only if I get stuck," Rafiq said, not looking up. "I always get stuck."

Lokesh, you think your Dada was always serious? When I was ten, in Meerut, our Hindi teacher Pandey-ji made each boy read aloud. I couldn't read fast. The letters seemed to jump about. So the first time I stumbled, I pulled my ears like a donkey and brayed. The whole class fell over laughing, and Pandey-ji laughed too.

After that I did it every time. Donkey, monkey, a crying baby. I was the funniest boy in school. Nobody knew I went home each day with my stomach in knots before reading class.

Then one day Pandey-ji kept me back and said, "Vikas, your donkey is very good. Now, can you read me this line without him?" Every afternoon for a month I read to him alone. Slowly the letters stopped jumping so much. And I didn't need the donkey any more.

Paulo stared at the rippling water. Abebe, holding the controller, stared at Paulo. Their teammate Sofia put a hand over her mouth.

Paulo laughed so hard he had to sit on the fountain's edge. Sofia was wheezing. It hurt, too: three weeks of work, dripping.

When the laughter faded, Paulo fished the drone out. "Okay. The demo resit is Friday. Sofia, check the motors. Abebe, the code. I'll dry the board." They carried it back to the lab like a wet cat.

Usha

I'm writing instead of saying this at the reunion lunch, because at the lunch you'd make it a joke, and we'd all laugh, and you'd be brilliant, as always.

You don't have to be funny with me. If something's hard, I'd really like to hear it. I'm free every evening this week, and I'll bring samosas.

Love,
Maria

Yusuf, you asked how George and I stayed married forty years. Let old Elizabeth tell you about our worst year. We were twenty-five, I a nervous young wife, in a rented room in Kochi, and the milk bills were piling up. Every time I tried to talk about money, George made a joke. "Money is a myth invented by milkmen." Very funny. I laughed, every time, and every time I felt a little smaller, as if my worry were childish.

One night I laid all the bills in a line on the floor and said, "George, I am not laughing tonight. I'm frightened, and I feel alone with this." He started a joke, looked at my face, and stopped. Then he sat down on the floor with me. We went through every bill until two in the morning.

He never lost his humour. He just learned when to put it down.

qa.a: Young Elizabeth felt dismissed and smaller each time, as if her worry were childish.

In the boys' hostel of the residential school in Dehradun, Vikas had painted "V + R = brothers for life" on the cupboard in September. Ramesh helped him with Sanskrit, shared his home-made laddoos, and stayed up when Vikas was homesick. "Best roommate in the whole school," Vikas told the warden.

Then, at football on Tuesday, Vikas slipped in the mud, and Ramesh laughed along with everyone else. Only for a second.

I'm Vidya, and in second year Joseph decided I was his whole world. "You're the only person in this college who actually understands me," he'd say on our walks round the hostel ground. I liked that. It felt special.

Then one night in November I missed his call. I was asleep; it was one in the morning. Next day he texted: "Knew it. You're like the rest. Useless when it counts." He told our group I was fake. I was completely bewildered. What had changed in one missed call?
